analysis.one_liner: Repeals dozens of federal tax breaks and ends the sale of public land resources below market value.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of the six committees it was referred to, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal roughly two dozen federal tax breaks benefiting the oil, gas, mining, timber, farming, insurance, publishing, and shipping industries, and would require the government to charge fair market value when selling public timber, minerals, grazing rights, water, and hydroelectric power. It would also put an 8 percent royalty and fee structure on mining claims on federal land and use the money to clean up abandoned mines. It was introduced by a single Democratic member with no cosponsors, referred to six committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently fund these subsidies and sell off public resources cheaply. Revenue from the repealed tax breaks, mining royalties, and fair-market fees would flow to the Treasury and to a fund for cleaning up abandoned mines, reducing deficits and public exposure to mine cleanup costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, hikers, and rural residents near public lands

how_it_helps.text: Title I repeals roughly two dozen federal tax breaks, including oil and gas drilling expensing, percentage depletion for oil, gas and mining, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and tax deferral for foreign subsidiaries of U.S. corporations.
Title II requires the government to sell timber, minerals, forage, federally owned water, and hydroelectric power at no less than fair market value, ending below-cost giveaways of public assets.

Mining on federal land, previously free of production royalties under the 1872 mining law, would owe an 8 percent royalty and an 8 percent severance tax, with the money dedicated to cleaning up abandoned mines and a $100 annual fee per mining claim.
Grazing on federal land would be priced at fair market value, below-cost timber sales from national forests would be banned, and patenting of new mining claims would be sharply limited.

analysis.who_pays: The companies that currently receive these tax breaks and below-market access to federal land and resources — oil and gas drillers, hardrock miners, timber companies, ranchers, and large farm operations — would pay higher taxes, royalties, and fees, some of which could be passed to consumers in energy and food prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, mining, timber, and agribusiness companies

drawbacks.text: Some provisions repeal incentives with public purposes of their own, such as credits for electric and clean-fuel vehicles, reforestation tax benefits, and the historic rehabilitation credit (which was cut, not repealed) — cutting these could slow adoption of cleaner technology and historic restoration, goals many subsidy critics share.

Repealing farm accounting provisions, cost-sharing exclusions, and the livestock feed assistance program would have raised costs and removed support for some smaller farmers, not only large agribusiness.

The bill authorized new user fees from beneficiaries of federal programs and an 8 percent royalty plus an 8 percent excise tax on mining, which industry would argue raises production costs that can be passed on to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains were real: billions in tax breaks and below-market resource giveaways to mining, energy, timber, and agriculture would have ended, with royalties and fair-market pricing replacing them and money dedicated to cleaning up abandoned mines. The main drawback is design, not principle: repealing some items (like clean-fuel and electric vehicle credits, reforestation incentives, and small insurance company tax rules) hits policies that arguably serve legitimate public goals, and ending farm cash-accounting and emergency feed assistance would have fallen partly on family-scale operations, not just agribusiness. A more targeted bill preserving genuinely useful incentives would have been stronger. Even so, the bill never received any hearing or vote, so its practical merits were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and various subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Corporate Welfare Elimination Act of 1999 on June 15, 1999.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to six committees — Ways and Means, Resources, Agriculture, Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Budget — and then to ten subcommittees over the following month.
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred; the last action was a subcommittee referral on July 13, 1999.
The bill expired with the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001, without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that receive the tax breaks and below-market public resources — oil and gas, mining, timber, grazing, agriculture, insurers, and exporters — kept everything the bill would have taken away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining, oil, timber, and farm subsidy recipients

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but attracted no cosponsors and no committee action followed.

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes, the record shows no party split — the bill simply never attracted support from either party.

industries.note: The bill repealed drilling and mining tax preferences and imposed an 8 percent royalty, an 8 percent severance tax, and a $100-per-claim annual fee on minerals taken from federal land. These industries currently extract public resources at little or no royalty under the 1872 mining law.

Below-cost timber sales from national forests would be banned and grazing fees set at fair market value, ending below-cost access to public land. Lower public-land costs come out of the Treasury, i.e., taxpayers.
The bill repealed farm tax accounting preferences, cost-sharing exclusions, and the emergency livestock feed assistance program, and cut payment limits for farmers receiving federal irrigation water.
Special tax treatment for Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations, the small life insurance company deduction, and the alternative tax for small property and casualty insurers would be repealed.
Foreign sales corporation tax exclusions and the Merchant Marine Capital Construction Fund tax deferral would be repealed, ending tax advantages for export income and shipbuilding finance.
Special tax treatment for magazine circulation spending and returns of magazines, paperbacks, and records would be repealed.
